content: The active ingredient must meet the specific identity test requirements. If the identity remains uncertain, it must also pass at least one additional confirmatory test. The formulation should be in the form of a fine powder, free from visible extraneous matter and hard lumps. It must be contained in a sealed, water-soluble bag. The suspension properties of the formulation must be tested using a suspension containing both the wettable powder (WP) and the bag material in the actual application ratio. This suspension should be prepared according to the specified procedure. After 30 minutes in CIPAC Standard Water D at 30 ± 2°C, a specified percentage of the formulation must remain in suspension. Persistent foam must be tested on a suspension containing the WP and the bag material in the actual application ratio, prepared in CIPAC Standard Water D. The maximum foam volume after one minute must not exceed the specified limit. The dissolution of the bag must be tested using a sample of the emptied and cleaned bag, along with an appropriate proportion of the WP, in CIPAC Standard Water D. The flow time of the resulting suspension must not exceed the specified limit. None of the tested bags should show signs of leakage or rupture during normal handling, both before and after storage. For record-keeping purposes, the suffix SB should be added to the formulation code (e.g., WP-SB). Sub-sampling of the bag should be done carefully to avoid damaging the seals. The contents of the bag should be transferred into a suitable flask for testing. The methods of analysis must comply with CIPAC, AOAC, or equivalent standards. If the methods are unpublished, full details and appropriate validation data must be submitted to FAO/WHO by the proposer. The formulation should be tested at the highest and lowest recommended rates of use, provided these do not exceed the conditions specified in the relevant method. Chemical assay is the most reliable method for measuring the mass of active ingredients in suspension. Simpler methods, such as gravimetric or solvent extraction, may be used routinely if they provide results equivalent to chemical assay. In case of dispute, chemical assay will serve as the referee method. The procedure for adding the bag material to the solution for suspension and foam tests involves preparing a stock solution of the bag material, dissolving it in standard water, and storing it in a stoppered bottle before use. The influence of seed treatment on germination is critical but not included in the specification due to the lack of a universal test method for all seed types. Users must strictly follow the manufacturer's recommendations and avoid treating seeds with unknown germination effects. Treated seeds should be stored in suitable containers, protected from excessive temperature and moisture. The formulation is expected to include a dye or pigment that permanently colors the seed after treatment. In some countries, specific colors may be legally required. The same color should not be used for denaturing seeds intended for livestock feed. Water-dispersible granules (WG) are designed for application after disintegration and dispersion in water using conventional spraying equipment. These granules are formulated in various ways depending on the active ingredient's properties and available manufacturing equipment. Products with a wide particle size range may segregate in containers, but the homogeneous nature of the mixture allows for a broader particle size range than typically used for granules. To evaluate the properties of WG according to a given specification, representative samples must be taken. A method for sample preparation (CIPAC MT 166) should be applied. If the material is packed in sealed water-soluble bags, samples of intact bags should be taken from freshly opened commercial containers, if possible. The formulation must be dry, free-flowing, nearly dust-free, and free from visible extraneous matter and hard lumps. It must also meet specific identity tests and comply with additional tests if the identity remains uncertain. The formulation's suspension properties, dustiness, and flow characteristics are essential for good field performance.
